transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I’m Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

I guess… what brings me in is this sadness I’ve been waking up with. It’s not just “I’m having a bad morning” sadness, it feels heavier than that, like this hollow place in my chest that’s already there before I even open my eyes.

I’m a dancer—well, choreography too—and usually I can feel something in me respond to music or movement, even on hard days. But lately it’s like the studio lights are on and everything looks the way it’s supposed to look, but there’s no music in me anymore. That sounds dramatic, I know, but that’s the closest way I can explain it. It’s like I’m present, but something that usually makes me feel alive just isn’t there.
Can you describe how long this feeling of sadness and lack of response to things you usually enjoy has been going on?

It’s been… about nine months, I think. Not every single minute in the exact same way, but the depressed part, the heaviness and that not-really-reaching-me feeling with things I normally love, that’s been there for around nine months now.

I keep trying to measure it by dance seasons or projects instead of calendar months, because that’s how my brain organizes time, but when I really count it out, it’s been most of the past year. Which feels strange to say out loud, because part of me keeps thinking, “No, it can’t have been that long,” but… it has.
Have you noticed any times during this past year when your mood felt unusually high, or you had much more energy than usual, maybe even more than you would expect for a good day?

Yes… yes, there were times like that. It’s a little embarrassing to say because at the time I didn’t think of it as “unusual,” I thought, finally, I’m back, I’m myself again. Like everything in me turned bright all at once.

I’d have these stretches where I felt almost dazzlingly alive, like my body was ahead of the music before the music even started. I’d get so certain about an idea or a plan, especially with choreography or what needed to happen next, and it felt obvious to me that everyone should just see it too. And then if someone questioned it—like if they said, “Maybe we should slow down,” or reminded me my ankle still needed rest—I could get suddenly furious. Not just annoyed. Furious in this sharp, instant way, like they were trying to take something away from me or dim the whole room.

And then later I’d think, why did I react like that? But in the moment it felt completely justified. It felt like I had this energy and clarity, and anyone interrupting it was the problem.
During those times when you felt unusually high or energized, did you find that you needed much less sleep than usual, like you could function well on just a few hours of sleep?

Yes… my sleep has been all over the place. During those higher-energy times, I’d stay up way too late, sometimes until dawn, sketching formations or reworking counts in my notebook like it was the most urgent thing in the world. It didn’t feel like normal insomnia exactly—more like I didn’t want to stop because everything was connecting, and if I went to sleep I’d lose it.

And then lately it’s different. I’ll fall asleep because I’m exhausted, but I wake up at four or five in the morning with my stomach tight, already tense before the day has even started. So it’s not one clean pattern. It’s like my body forgot how to do sleep normally.

latest_inference.note: The patient described both depressive episodes lasting over two weeks and clear manic episodes, including increased energy, decreased need for sleep, and impaired judgment during those times. This rules out recurrent depressive disorders (F33.2) and supports a diagnosis of bipolar disorder, currently with mixed features or recent manic and depressive episodes. F31.3 (Bipolar disorder, current episode depressed, moderate) is ruled out because the patient has had a recent manic episode, making F31.4 (Bipolar disorder, current episode manic with psychotic features or severe) more accurate based on the elevated mood and behavioral changes described.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a clear pattern of alternating depressive and manic episodes, fulfilling criteria for Bipolar I Disorder, Current Episode Mixed. The depressive symptoms include anhedonia, persistent sadness, and loss of joy in a previously vital activity (dance). The manic symptoms include elevated mood, increased energy, decreased need for sleep, and impaired judgment during high periods.
